title: 3.2.10 Plain English to Pseudocode: Tracing Parameter Values
description: Turn plain-English steps into pseudocode for a program that passes base into showPriceWithTax(price), then decides Over budget or Within budget from the same base.

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** Set `base` to `100`.

**2.** Call `showPriceWithTax` with `base`. Inside the call the value becomes the parameter `price` and the function prints the price with tax. You do not write what happens inside.

**3.** After the call, check whether `base` is over `80`.

**4.** If it is, print `Over budget`.

**5.** Otherwise, print `Within budget`.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: the double-rail box is the call, and the diamond after it tests the same `base`.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `SET lives TO 3` (start a value)
- `CALL greet WITH name` (use a function)
- `IF lives is 0` ... `ELSE` ... `END IF` (a check with two ways out, steps inside indented)
- `OUTPUT lives` (show something)

Plain English is fine here. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, trace it twice by hand: once with `base` at 100 and once pretending it is 50. The call runs both times, and only the answer after the diamond changes.
hints: The call comes before the check, on the one route every run takes.
The check uses `base`, not `price`: `price` only exists inside the function.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: Sets base to 100
requirements.description: Set base to 100 before anything uses it.
requirements.hint: Add a step that sets base to 100.

requirements.title: Calls the function with base
requirements.description: Call showPriceWithTax and pass it base.
requirements.hint: Write a step that calls showPriceWithTax and passes it base.

requirements.title: The call comes before the decision
requirements.description: Call the function first, then make the decision.
requirements.hint: Put the call step before the step that checks against 80.

requirements.title: The decision tests base against 80
requirements.description: The check asks whether base is over 80.
requirements.hint: Check whether base is over 80, using base itself.

requirements.title: Each answer prints the right message
requirements.description: Over budget for yes, Within budget for the other way out.
requirements.hint: Print Over budget when the check is yes, and Within budget on the other way out (ELSE).

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program is: set base to 100; call showPriceWithTax with base (inside the call the value becomes the parameter price and it prints the price with tax; the body is not written out); then check whether base is over 80; if so print "Over budget", otherwise print "Within budget". Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, CALL, IF, ELSE, END IF, OUTPUT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite, for example checking against 80 before the call for the ordering criterion. Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
